utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing to delay us, may the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, good morning to you, sir. Before Mr. Zecevic resumes his --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Mr. Zecevic resumes his cross-examination, I remind you, you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Planojevic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, yesterday we discussed the sending of certain inspectors in the field. We mentioned Danilo Vukovic. That was the question where we left it off. We discussed the decision by virtue of which he was dispatched in the field. In addition to him, there was also Dragan Andan, another inspector who was sent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you 1D00-0617. The document is dated 23 July 1992. It is an authorisation issued to Dragan Andan to tour the security services centres, public security stations, and police stations on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He will inspect them, monitor them their work, offer expert assistance, and suggest measures for the improvement of shortcomings observed. Signed: For Mico Stanisic. Can you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlastimir Kusmuk, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of such an authorisation issued to Dragan Andan in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Dragan Andan left in early July on same business. I don't know whether he had received that authorisation by that time. Actually, I think it was already in June when he went out in the field for the first time, and I think Danilo and he worked as a team. I was wasn't competent for any uniformed police issues, but I do know that the two of them left together. I don't know whether they had any written authorisation before there date, but I know they were dispatched earlier than the date referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll wait for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan stayed in Sarajevo for a while and then he was banned from entering the republican SUP building of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And during that time, he had no assignments. And we made use of him to carry out such visits, when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to speak slowly, because we are missing a part of your answer because of that reason. When you say that Danilo left, you have in mind Danilo Vukovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is the inspector whom we discussed yesterday towards the end of the session; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that in your opinion this authorisation we are looking at is actually the second visit by Dragan Andan or the second inspection of the CSBs and public security stations in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am positive that he did the same in June. Therefore, I believe this was his second inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D392, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, the inspectors Radenko Vujicic and Petar Kovacevic, were they part of your administration or some other?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not in my administration, in the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. During examination last Friday, my learned friend showed you a document which is 1D84. It is your letter, signed by you, dated the 5th of June, 1992, sent to all CSBs in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D84. Or P568; the documents are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therein, you state that you have observed an increase in crime, especially property crime, as well as war crimes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you provide instructions to use strong measures, as well as to take people into custody if they were perpetrators of all types of crime. That information was issued to all employees, whereby you also invited them to cooperate with the judiciary and the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in the most is the suggestion you make in the penultimate sentence, which reads: "In wartime, you will encounter numerous obstacles in combatting crime and will, on occasion, be unable to take on adequate measures; in such cases, record all information in Official Notes for subsequent measures, i.e., criminal prosecution ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are sitting here as the author of the document. At the time, having in mind the situation in the field and the events taking place in wartime circumstances, you could foresee that the members of the police will face serious obstacles in conducting investigations of certain types of crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of their obligations, based on legal regulation, as well as other laws and regulations regulating the work of the organs of the interior according to which they have to undertake certain, as you call them here, adequate measures, still, there was a possibility, with a view to the situation in the field, that such measures would not be implemented; they wouldn't be able to do so. You could see that much at that stage?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In such cases, your instruction, or the instruction of the ministry, rather, was that they gather all information and include them in Official Notes, or by any other means, so as to enable when the conditions became more favourable to conduct or put in place adequate measures and prosecute the perpetrators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, your instructions had absolutely nothing to do with any covering up or implementing inadequate measures. You actually directed your men to apply the only measures that they could, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no other way to go about it, other than to approach it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you discussed certain flexibility on the part of the Ministry of the Interior, you had in mind this type of flexibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Flexibility in the sense of applying measures which may not be absolutely adequate but are the only ones possible, given the circumstances at the time.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I can clarify. For example, there's a crime that had been committed but you cannot investigate it because you cannot go about putting questions and investigating because it is a war. Once the conditions are better, then can you carry out your operational measures. In times of combat, you could not even approach the front lines, and the entire Sarajevo area was one large front line. There was combat all over, throughout the war, especially in Ilidza and Vogosca. There wouldn't go -- there wouldn't be a week that would go by without combat; this includes Hadzici as well. The only part that was partially spared was Pale. There were two corps there - the Sarajevo and Zenica Corps - facing the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The manning strength was about 100.000 versus the 18.000 of the soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. If there was a single company out of combat, it's already a problem. And it's particularly difficult to document anything in such conditions. We have scene-of-crime measures which we could not apply in combat -- in the combat environment. Having in mind such a complex situation, on one hand the shortage of soldiers -- because everyone went to the front lines, even those who missed a limb. Everyone was in the trenches, because people were fighting for their bare lives. That is why this dispatch was fashioned in this way. But the purposes of it was not to instruct people to oversee or forget something. I hope that you can at least partially understand what my intention was, since I authored this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I thank you for this comprehensive explanation. Sir, when you were examined on Friday, you were shown another document, or, rather, another version of this document. There were questions put to you about the signature. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I won't go through it all again; I believe that was cleared up. But what was key was that both versions we have in the file - and you have explained why they are different - have the same content.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Except the word "for." It was simply copied twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "for," you mean in the signature block?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D85, which is the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was sent by the CSB in Banja Luka to its regional stations. You viewed this document on Friday as well, I believe. It conveys the entirety of your dispatch, of your instructions, does it not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And here it's in quotation marks. We have it all here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And towards the end, the chief of the centre added another instruction of his own, saying that all authorised officials should be acquainted with this dispatch and that they should abide by the instructions provided. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can go to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct then?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, this document was drafted in early June 1992. In mid-July, the first collegium meeting was held on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know of that first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P160.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall having seen this document? It is of the 11th of July, and you were in attendance at this collegium session; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 16, I believe, in e-court. It is -- it is 0324-1863; that's the ERN number. I am afraid I omitted to check what the English page is. That is why I read out the ERN number. I apologise. Thank you. This is exactly what I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Mico Stanisic's presentation. I'll just read out two or three things to you to check if you remember. In the centre - I believe it's the fourth paragraph - it says: "The Ministry of the Interior is a professional organisation, that is, a professional police without political influence," and so on. Do you remember that was the position of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes. I'm sure I cannot reproduce the exact words that he said, but I remember that he advocated such a professional attitude all the time, and even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to page 20 of the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which is your discussion at this collegium meeting. You asked a few questions and made some suggestions; they are listed here, as you see. And what matters most to me here is that you mention documenting war crimes, medical records, and so on, as a priority. And you say that lists of war criminals must be made distributed to the centres. Mr. Planojevic, I believe that when you gave the interview in 2004 - and I think that you repeated as much on Friday - you said that this document doesn't mention your words, and that's a point you insisted on. Namely, that the priority is documenting war crimes. And you added that this applied to everybody, irrespective of the ethnicity or the religious affiliation of the perpetrators or the victims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll read out some more conclusions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's on page 23 of the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see conclusion number 1 refers to -- or, rather, explains the complexity of the situation the MUP of the RS was in, the personnel strength, and the fact that the police was resubordinated to the military in the conduct of combat operations, or, in other words, it's involved in combat. But even so, it is insisted that all members of the MUP take measures from their remit to ensure the establishment and the functioning of the authorities, as well as to secure the personal safety and the security of property of the citizens. Do you remember that this, in rough terms, was the position of the MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 26, and these are conclusions 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see that one of the conclusions of that meeting, that is, the collegium held on the 11th of July, stems from your suggestion, which is the preventation [as interpreted] and the documenting of war crimes with these of -- all legally prescribed means and methods, as well as filing criminal complaints and so on. And then item 7 reads: The prevention and detection of other criminal offences, irrespective of the identity of the perpetrators. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P427.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After this meeting on the 11th of July, a notification was sent out about some aspects of the activities taken so far and future tasks. The date is 11 July 1992, and it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: 17 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- and it was sent to the president and the prime minister. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Such notifications or reports were mostly a task of the analysis department of the minister.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That analysis department did all such work, especially for the cabinet and the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then it's not surprising that you're not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After this meeting, there was your dispatch of 5 June, regarding war crimes. Then there is your suggestion, the discussion, and the conclusions reached at the collegium to prosecute the perpetrators of war crimes and any other crimes, irrespective of who the perpetrators or the victims were. Then on 19 July a form was submitted, which I'm about to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D63.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember drafting a form for the identification of war criminals?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I may clarify. We established a group of operatives whose only task was to be of the prevention and detection of war crimes. I sat down with them, and we made a rough outline of that future questionnaire and what it should contain. There was Milomir Orasanin, Nenad Skipina, and, I believe, Petko Pekic. It wasn't ready for the meeting though, but two of these people soon were transferred to other jobs after my resignation. But their only task was coordinating such activities. But, as I said, Pekic went to the police, Orasanin went to the border, and Pekic went elsewhere, so nobody was left from that original group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify. If I understood you well, this group which was established was part of your administration.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when you said that it dealt with war crimes, generally speaking, I must ask you once more: We are talking about war crimes, no matter who the victims or the perpetrators were; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the beginning of his answer. We didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Kindly speak slowly. The interpreters did not understand your answer. Could you please repeat slowly. You answered "absolutely," and then ...

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say we didn't care who the victim was, it was only important that it was a war crime. I can mention an example: The only two cases, detention cases, that is, persons who were taken in, were documented for murdering non-Serbs. So this goes to show that this wasn't just hollow talk. And this was -- this happened in the areas where we could go at the time, Vrace and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said Grbavica and Vrace. So that's a part of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were areas where we could function normally, where we could physically go. And when I say "normal," I mean that we were, indeed, present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you page 3 of this document, the form itself, and I would like a brief comment. We were saying that war crimes were prosecuted no matter who the victims were, that is, irrespective of their ethnicity or religious affiliations. We see items 5 and 6 of this form for victims of war crimes. Item 5 reads: ethnicity; and 6, religion. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It can be seen plainly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, counsel for Mr. Stanisic has put to you a whole string of documents which all seem to bare proof of the intention by the MUP to have all crimes properly registered, irrespective of the perpetrator or the victim, and including war crimes; and the document that we have on the screen before us now certainly confirms this. But it is also, as you may know, a common experience in real life that one thing is the written word, quite a different thing is, sometimes, the reality. So my question to you is if can you tell us whether the intention that we have seen documented here were carried out in practical life? Is it your impression that, indeed, all war crimes, or at least most of the war crimes, were, in fact, registered and investigated and prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? I cannot state anything with certainty, because we saw what it was like in Vogosca yesterday when the chief said what he said. The general commitment and the intention of at least the people who were on the collegium was what can be seen from the documents. I didn't speak about other things. I don't know if I should mention this. One highly esteemed attorney was here often. He was not a Serb, and he lived in the area of Grbavica, and we protected his property in the same way and filed criminal complaints. I didn't want to mention everything. Unfortunately, he did suffer some adverse consequences later. But often people became victims, but given the circumstances, I think that we did more than many others would have. I don't know if you're satisfied or if I should clarify further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I guess this is as close as we can get to this matter. Back to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to follow up on this. If I understand correctly, it is your position that the MUP headquarters, or the MUP leadership, did absolutely everything they could, given the circumstances at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can state that with regard to the period in question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you have direct knowledge about it because you worked at MUP headquarters at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore -- or, let me rephrase it. Do you have reason to believe that elsewhere in the territory MUP members worked differently?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems they did, once -- or now that I know how the situation developed. There must have been people who did not adhere to these principles. I didn't know that at the time though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, that the official position was not that negative incidents should be covered up; on the contrary, that they must be registered, in order to take adequate measures once the conditions allow it. Did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And for all serious crimes, we had to conduct an on-site investigation. And if you did that, and if there is no investigating judge at the site, then it is forwarded - I mean, the criminal complaint - and it cannot be closed until the perpetrator is found. That's why we conducted on-site investigations, because we wanted to reach the judicial bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to a set of other topics which you discussed with my learned friend on Friday. You'll recall having discussed -- or, rather, my learned friend put you a question to which you answered about the competences of the police, should the police come across a perpetrator who is a member of the military. You confirmed that in peacetime conditions, as should have been the case in the time of the war, if the police come across a perpetrator of a crime who is a member of the military, they were supposed to hold him until the arrival of the military organs who would then take him over and prosecute further.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, this has a practical consequence or implication. What we are discussing, what we were discussing so far, were the theoretical presumptions. However, in reality, if a member of the military committed a crime, they were usually accompanied by others. Seldom did it happen that a single member of the military committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it also frequently took place at night when people were not moving about and you simply couldn't know who the perpetrator was. It was quite customary to have a curfew introduced in such periods of war. Only uniformed personnel moving to the lines went around at that particular time of day, and this further makes the discovering of perpetrators more difficult. And, of course, they were usually not alone. They moved in groups. I'll cite two examples, for you to understand this more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But do it slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Rudo, a soldier left the line and killed the brigade commander, his own soldier killed him. There were simply psychopaths around. They were able to do anything, let alone kill their commander. And there were a number of such examples. Just imagine a policeman bringing in a person like that. That was life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You foresaw my next question, actually. It is a fact that members of the army in wartime conditions, by nature of things, are armed; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If the police went by their operational rules, when there was an arrest of a person who is suspected of carrying arms and was ready to use them, then such actions were planned with care, involving a number of personnel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The crux of the matter is that the Ministry of the Interior was obliged to protect its members. Every life lost in line of duty is an irreparable loss for the organisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, my learned friend also asked you about the way members of the Ministry of the Interior were disciplined. You know that the Law on the Interior was issued in March 1992; we discussed that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that law came into force on the 30th of March, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We said yesterday that it was almost identical to the Law on the Interior of the SFRY. Or, actually, of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The law foresaw the existence of certain disciplinary instances such as disciplinary commissions and disciplinary prosecutors; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At a certain point in his examination, my learned friend Mr. Hannis asked you about certain disciplinary procedures and the removal of certain heads of SJBs. You said that you were not aware of such a removal of any of the chiefs being replaced during that time. Do you recall that answer of yours?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that in 1992 the chief of the Bijeljina CSB, Mr. Jesoric, was removed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at least three SJB chiefs in Bijeljina were removed: Mr. Pantic, Mr. Devedlaka, and even Andan for a while, who was in that position?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Mr. Devedlaka went there to establish -- to introduce some order, and I believe it was in May. I remember him appearing at a collegium meeting in Belgrade, and he said that he wouldn't go back to Bijeljina at any cost because that was the level of threat issued against him. I think he was, at the time, the chief of the station, and I believe he simply appeared at that meeting. I know, however, that the station chiefs were then changed, because it was discussed in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Andan was appointed to that position later?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know and I believe that he was the chief of the station. I only know that he was in Bijeljina, but I'm not sure anymore whether he was a chief of the CSB or the station there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in Teslic the SJB chief was also removed; another person assumed that position?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned that when discussing it with Mr. -- with the Prosecutor. I believe I learned that from Zivkovic or some other work-mates of mine. But that was as late as 1993 or 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That was when you learned about that, in 1993 or 1994?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, the removal took place in 1992, and you -- they were -- they confirmed it to you later on?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zivkovic told me that when he came to the administration, when we discussed certain events at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the chief of the Zvornik SJB was removed after the operation carried out to bring in the Yellow Wasps; another person was brought in instead?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because I know the first chief. Later on, we became friends. His name is Dragan Spasojevic. He told me. I think he was the initial chief who was then removed. I even think that someone from Loznica came there and declared themselves commander or chief of their own will, and I believe such a situation continued for about two months. I think that person was a boxer or something. In any case, all that information is something I learned in discussions with other people who were, for the most part, participants in those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Hence, your question [as interpreted] that this was not happening could be simply interpreted as you not being familiar with it at the time. But now you know that in 1992 some SJB chiefs and CSB chiefs were actually removed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I wasn't aware of any of that. I learned of those things later on, through conversations with people I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 20, line 5, I believe I said "your answer," whereas in the transcript it reads "your question."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, it was your answer given to the Prosecutor on Friday. Let me ask you this: We mentioned Boro Maksimovic, and we saw some reports of your employees about how he looked down upon the MUP and the CSB, not allowing anyone to interfere with his personnel policy, and so on and so forth. Did you know that he received a decision, disciplinary decision, to be suspended from work on the 15th of the October, 1992? And then the CSB chief, on the 30th of November, even filed a criminal complaint, a criminal report against him. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D186.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the document. And since you weren't aware of that event, I simply wanted to indicate to you -- excuse me? Yes. In the file, we have both the disciplinary decision and the criminal report. I just wanted to show you the first page. The same goes for Vlado Kelovic, who was station commander in Vogosca. He also had a disciplinary decision issued in his case on suspension on the 15th of October, and a criminal report against him was submitted in November 1992. I suppose you weren't aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 1D187, for ease of reference. Both documents are in tabs 124 and 125.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Since we discussed Dragan Andan, did you know that he, too, was suspended at a certain point in time, in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan, himself, told me that upon his arrival. I believe it was late 1992, when he came to Bijeljina. He said that the minister removed him, and he complained that it wasn't done properly. I don't know more than that. But he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is P1269, tab 126, for reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While on the topic of Dragan Andan and Bijeljina, tell me if you heard of the military camp at Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of its existence, but I don't know under whose competence it was. I think it existed throughout the war. I don't know whether it was a prison or a camp, but I think it was in operation throughout the war. If it's a camp, it's a camp. But I don't know what its proper name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was called a military camp for POWs.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. But I did know of its existence and that it operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic [sic], is there a particular reason why you added this document to your list as -- under tab 126? Obviously it is already under tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay. It's no problem. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... mistake. It's a mistake. I wasn't aware that it was under tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I added it this morning. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You remember that on Friday you discussed the road through Caparde with my learned friend. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence, you confirmed, then, that the road was not safe, that you couldn't drive down that road safely; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was unsafe throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that the MUP, in July or August, lost two of its members on that road, Trobok and Spajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were telecom experts. They were members of the state security, but they were helping out the public security. They wanted to keep communications lines running but they both got killed. One them of had a doctoral degree. He was a professor. I believe he even spent some time in America and got his doctorate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, in July or August, they were ambushed and got killed; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their vehicle was hit from a hand-held rocket-launcher and they burnt in their car on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was because of such ambushes traffic on that road was organised in convoys, at the head of which there was an armed military vehicle, and that's how people drove down that road?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But that wasn't safe either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remember that the name of Dusko Malovic was mentioned in your evidence on Friday. You confirmed that that unit from Sokolac was on the front line in Grbavica in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were holding the line by the school, which isn't even a hundred metres away from the building we were in. That was the part of the line that they held. And occasionally they would take part in combat operations, when there was more intensive fighting. Of course, you don't stay at the line all the time. You're -- you're relieved from time to time. I mentioned an incident in Dobrinja by some garages. One man was killed, and one was wounded. And upon returning to the school, they talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they were ordered by the minister on 15 June 1992 - that unit, namely - to mobilize recruits in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you document P1422. You see that the order is signed -- well, the signature looks like that of Cedo Kljajic to me, but maybe you can say who it is. It says: "For the minister."

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make it out. The first letter is K, but I can't see the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Here the unit is ordered to act upon the decision of the Presidency on general and public mobilization of 20 May 1992. And on the 15th of June, they are ordered to mobilize conscripts in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, and it also says that the mobilization shall start on 16 June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While you were at Vrace, you saw that unit daily -- or, rather, they were in front of the school at Vrace; that's where they held the line.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would mostly meet them in the cafeteria during our meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that until June they had their positions there, since that member of theirs got killed in Dobrinja in June; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. You know how it is when you lose a comrade. It gets very emotional. It may have been in July even. But it's well known when there was fighting. He was hit by sniper by the garages. It may have been around the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remembered the incident involving Ivan Curak, a Croat, a -- who was a citizen of Sarajevo. He had a sniper rifle. And you saw Dusko Malovic beating or mistreating him. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He hit him, and that's what I said. It was near the gate at -- in the duty officers' room. So it can easily be observed when you walk past.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This may jog your memory, if I told you that on that day one police officer guarding the school at Vrace was killed by sniper, and the assumption was that the shot had come from the building where this Curak lived and that's why the unit went there and took in a person who had a rifle with a sniper sight. Do you -- wouldn't you then remember the context of the event?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The search was, indeed, carried out, because a person got killed. I believe the neighbourhood was called Shopping, and they were high-rise residential buildings. And it's on Leninova Street. One man was injured. His name was Ned; I don't remember his last name. Another was killed. They were by the gate at the entrance. And a sniping rifle and a Colt were found during the search. But as I knew the person, I said that it was impossible that he could have done so. The reason was that they thought this man was the perpetrator because he had such a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is a founded suspicion, isn't it, two persons were hit by a sniper and that man was in possession of a sniping rifle?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I only have two more questions, sir, and I believe then we can finish. Irrespective of the -- the clash that you were involved in in 1992 and your resignation from your position, when Mico Stanisic returned to be minister again in 1994 - for a very brief period though - he invited you to return to public security. He explicitly asked you to finish the work that you started in 1992 about all crimes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if I may explain. I was informed that he was looking for me, and I believe that we again met at the Bistrica hotel. What a coincidence. At the time, I was very unaware of some other things that had happened. It was a "import of oil." Some 5 or 6 million German marks were transferred to Bulgaria for the importation of oil, I believe. That was what happened. But neither the oil nor the money ever arrived. And then there was aluminum from Nevesinje; the sum involved was some 14 million, I believe. So the question was: Are you willing to continue where you left off, because the conditions are much more favourable now. You can do it. But then he told me about these other things. As you know, I refused, and I never again got the idea to go back. And I know that these were high-scale cases and difficult to deal with even in a well-organised and functioning state. I mentioned that there was an attempt to establish an administration to combat the undermining of the economic foundation of the state, and it was owing to me that it was not established. So he told me that I would be free in my selection of personnel, and I had carte blanche; but it was my conviction that there would be no changes, and I told him my opinion frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, apart from these large-scale embezzlement and other cases, he told you that you could finish doing what you started in 1992 concerning all crimes, but it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. We spoke very long. I believe that it was past midnight when we finished. We discussed many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you, sir, that in 1994, during his second term in office, Mr. Stanisic was provided security by the unit of Dusko Malovic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question to me? Well, probably, but I'm not sure. I saw, then, that they escorted him in a combat lineup. When we went to that collegium in Belgrade; that's when it happened. Then there was a misunderstanding, because some people may have -- may have thought that I was lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Planojevic. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Krgovic, do you stand by your position that you decline to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, it's a few minutes before the break, so we would take the break at this point and you would re-examine when we return.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be convenient for me. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, with your permission - I spoke to my friend, Mr. Hannis. I noticed that a part of yesterday's transcript which I recall witness gave the answer was not recorded. And I spoke to Mr. Hannis, if he would be so kind to let me clarify this with the witness before he starts his re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And I will, if you allow, have a -- first a follow-up question on something you mentioned just before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just before the break, Mr. Zecevic asked you this: "If I understood correctly, apart from these large-scale embezzlement and case he told you could" - and "he" is Mr. Stanisic - "told you that you could finish doing what you started in 1992 concerning all crimes ..." And you answered: "Yes, correct." Do I understand correctly that Mr. Stanisic told you that you could do your work on all crimes except on these large-scale, that they were excluded from your work, if you would have accepted? Is that how I should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It referred to everything that was happening then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So even those special cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He especially stressed these. I didn't even know about that. And he informed me what had happened in the meantime, these large-scale cases. I didn't even know about them. And he explained to me how it all happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, yesterday's transcript, on page 6, doesn't show part of your answer. I would like you to repeat your answer. You remember that Mr. Hannis asked you about the meeting you attended in February 2009, I believe, in Nedzarici in Sarajevo, the meetings with the representatives of the OTP; remember?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You then informed the OTP that in the meantime you had had a contact a few months earlier with Mr. Stanisic. And Mr. Stanisic then told you that he is familiar with the contents of your statement given to the OTP in 2004. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You then said that Mr. Stanisic, at that meeting, asked you if you were willing to be a Defence witness regarding the events -- the events in Sarajevo before the war; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it is correct that Mr. Stanisic asked you that in December 2008?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was earlier than that, but I'm not sure. Let me try and focus. But it doesn't matter. But he asked me, if necessary was I willing, especially with regard to this aspect, because I was involved in many events; and I said, If necessary, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- good morning, Mr. Planojevic. I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- start off first with questions you were asked today. And I want to begin with just a follow-up on what Judge Delvoie asked you when we came back in. If I understand correctly, Mr. Stanisic was offering you a job and giving you carte blanche to investigate all crimes, it sounds like; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are fully correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us why you declined? Because it sounds like a great job. And if there's something about the answer that causes you concerns, we could ask the Judges to go in private session if you're concerned about mentioning a name or something. But, otherwise, if you feel free to speak about it in open session, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of my previous experience with the media, I will try to steer clear of mentioning any names. But I'll try to explain why I declined the offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, we would rather not concern ourselves with what the media might think or might not think. It's more important that you tell the full truth. So if you feel more comfortable by going into private session to give this reply to the Prosecution's question, I suggest we do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so you understand, in private session that won't be broadcast and picked up by the media.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think even without me mentioning any specific names my clarification will suffice for you to understand. I'd rather not put my faith in the hands of a private session either. Or perhaps if I received some assurance that what I say here will not leave this room. But, in any case, once I explain, I believe you will realize that there's no need for me to mention names. May I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The operational staff was decimated at the time. Such personnel was always in small numbers, but when the body of such personnel split between the three ethnicities, you simply found yourself in a situation where you had a serious shortage of men. Secondly, as I said, almost half of all men left abroad within a year. Thirdly, a lot of those working in the crime department had already left for the uniformed police because they realized that it was far easier to act as a chief in the border police than stay in the crime department. There was another thing, which was the war. Small, ordinary men could not influence great changes. Those who had material, economic influence were involved. I even know the name of the people who took the money for Bulgaria. I think there was a certain lady, Detricka [phoen], on their side, and I won't mention any names on our side. But when you come across such a situation even in a most organised state, it's difficult to deal with it. And we didn't even have the most primitive technical equipment we could employ. Then there was the war, which didn't last a couple of months, but a few years by that point in time. I realized that there were new people coming on board who were better placed to assist. For example, Pale is a small location with perhaps a population of 10.000. After the war, I think it had about ten or a dozen murders out of only two -- of which only two were actually -- had their perpetrators prosecuted, irrespective of the ethnicity of the victims. So I realized on time what was looming ahead. I was simply brought up and educated in a different fashion, and I received professional training. When we say "social self-protection," it's an old concept as part of which the citizens were willing to report things to the policemen. If you recall the murder and attempted murder of the Turkish ambassador, it were the citizens who were chasing the perpetrators. They didn't mind that the person was armed; whereas today you can't even get a piece of information out of anyone. Between 1994 and now, it's only been 16 years, but people no longer have any trust in the police. And it was for those reasons, being aware of what time was to come, that I deadlined. After the war, I received a number of similar offers from ministers and deputy ministers. I always deadlined because with my mental framework I always believed there was far more to lose for me than to gain. I hope this explains my position a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of interventions in the transcript, just for the clarity. I mean, if you want me ... 32, 1, the witness -- it's recorded: "Small, ordinary men could not influence great changes." I believe the -- the witness said the small ordinary man were not capable of conducting such crimes. That was my understanding. Maybe can you clarify that with the witness. 32, 7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Microphone not activated] ... I see he's nodding his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... could we deal with them one at a time, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I see he's nodding his head in affirmative. So I'll take that as a yes from the witness, that what you've said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may -- may I deal with -- with -- with the witness on this? Thank you, Mr. Hannis. [Interpretation] Sir, a few corrections for the transcript. At page 32, line 1, you said small ordinary people were not the ones who commit those crimes. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because they couldn't even find themselves in a position to do that. Only those who were financially powerful could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just go slowly so that the interpreters could catch up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is fine. Page 32, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, please. Go on. My question to the witness would be: What crimes are we really talking about here? But that's another -- that's -- that's a different issue as the one you're raising. So please proceed. And I apologise for intervening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can deal with that also, Your Honours, if you want me to do. But I would like first to clarify the transcript, if possible. [Interpretation] Page 32, line 7. You said -- well, what's recorded is -- just a moment. I think you said that such investigations of such serious crimes would last a few months or years. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I wanted to say. Not only a few months but a few years, meaning that it couldn't be concluded within months, a few months. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there seems to be something on the record about the war, whereas I don't think you said that. When you discussed Pale, you said after the war -- first you discussed the population of 10.000, and then you said that after the war there were ten to 12 murders. After the war - you probably meant after 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you said that that was not a matter of ethnicity, because all victims were Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And, still, nothing was done on resolving those crimes -- or, rather, something was done, but it wasn't followed through. Sorry. There was the chief and deputy chief of the centre involved, the most responsible persons in question dealing with that; whereas, the chief was actually liquidated in Sarajevo in 1999, I think. And before that, the deputy chief of the centre was also killed. So no matter what the effort that you invest, even to date it didn't develop. It didn't go anywhere. And that is, I think, why I didn't want to discuss it openly. It was my assessment that, actually, things would develop the way they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, you're speeding up, because there's another clarification. Line 35 -- line 6, page 35: You said that is why I declined, meaning the offer made to you in 1994 as well as a number of other offers you received from ministers or deputy ministers. Is that correct? That's what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you, Your Honours. I clarified this part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Planojevic, for your explanation. And if you have any long answers to any of my coming questions, when you give those long answers please try to remember to speak slowly. Thank you. First thing today at page 3, Mr. Zecevic was asking about Dragan Andan. And your answer was recorded as: "Dragan stayed in Sarajevo for a while and then he was banned from entering the republican SUP building ..." Can you tell me when that was? What year, what time-period?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. I returned from Belgrade on the 27th of May, I believe. I found Dragan at the headquarters in Vrace. He told me -- I don't know whether Jusuf Pusina was the minister at the time, but apparently he prohibited him from the entering -- from entering the building of the republican ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then he came to Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So this was the -- not the Serb MUP; this was the Bosnian MUP building?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Andan had not joined the Serbian MUP before the 27th of May; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned, he was already there. But I think he came out on the 9th of May, or left, because on that day about a dozen people from the federal ministry in Sarajevo arrived in Vrace, five or six of which were from the crime department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I understand. Next, at page 4 and going on to page 5, you were asked about your 5 June dispatch that you sent out to all the CSBs - that's P568 and 1D84 - about start fighting crime now and send in your dispatches and make Official Notes. The Official Notes that you mention in there being written to record information about crimes, if -- if nothing more could be done because of the circumstances, where would or should such Official Notes have been sent? Would those go to your administration or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such notes are not sent anywhere. They are part and parcel of case files, of particular case files, so as to enable anyone to have a full insight into the case at any point in time. Perhaps another explanation. Information need not only be recorded by way of notes. For the most part, verbal statements can be put into notes. But this also includes other evidence. I did mention notes specifically because most of it could be obtained by speaking with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at is to find out whether you, in your administration, would have received any of that kind of information about war crimes committed by Serbs against non-Serbs. Would you have received any Official Notes or reports in your administration; or was that information that would have remained at the CSB or the SJB, where the investigation was done?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, daily bulletins would be used in order to inform those higher up. There was no need, save for exceptionally difficult situations, to communicate directly, because then only that would be done, given the small number of personnel. If more difficult cases are concerned, then assistance was needed. I explained the role of the administration. One of the tasks was also to professionally assist through direct contact with the inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 10, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the document that is the record of the 11 July meeting in Belgrade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he said that in your interview in 2004 you had pointed out that that document doesn't have all your words that you said at the meeting about emphasizing documenting war crimes as a priority. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you see that document in 1992, the record of the meeting? I assumed that you did not.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why your words "emphasizing reporting war crimes" were left out?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one looks at that document - we can put it up on the screen, if you so wish - one can see that it says "summary" of the meeting, meaning that it summarized the comments made. So that part didn't find its way in. I saw the document for the first time in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 18 today, you were asked some questions about whether you were aware of certain MUP officials being removed, SJB chiefs. And, in particular, at this page you were asked about Predrag Jesoric being removed at the Bijeljina CSB. My question is: Did -- do you know what position he went to after he was head of CSB in 1992? Did you know he was head of the department for foreigners, travel documents, and border crossing?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see that for myself in 1994 or 1995, because I had to get in touch with Jesoric for some reason. Perhaps in a conversation then he told me how it came about, but I can't recall any details. I know that he worked on those jobs, but I don't know whether it was 1994 or 1995 when we got in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I could pull that up, but I think you'll see in the July 11th meeting, 1992, he's referred to by that position at that time. Would you disagree?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything. I know he was removed, although I don't know when. I also know that Pantic was at the meeting, although I don't know in what capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you have an opinion as to whether a move from the CSB chief position in Bijeljina to being head of this department would be considered a lateral move, a promotion, a demotion? Do you have an opinion?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not even certain whether that department existed at the time. In any case, the level of department within an administration is significantly lower than the level of a CSB chief. If we were to put it in terms of hierarchy, perhaps the head of centre and the head of administration would be at an approximately same level. Or maybe the administration chief would be a bit higher up, but only within his specific remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked about the SJB chief in Teslic being removed. Do you know who that person was by name that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I think I mentioned that in the context of the Green Berets, and then I said that Zivkovic told me about certain problems he and the chief of the centre had. It could be around the time or in the context of the removal of the station chief. I know there were some removals there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said you mentioned that in the context of Green Berets. Was that Green Berets or Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I mention the name Kezunovic. Does that name ring a bell as the chief of Teslic who was removed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of Dragan Kezunovic, but that's not the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware that the chief that was removed was later reinstated in 1992, in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. But I do know that in Teslic, because of the significant problems there, perhaps in 1993, a governmental commission was established, and I was a member of it. It all had to do with illegal trafficking on large scale, and there were clashes between the then-Municipal Assembly speaker and the chief of the station. After those meetings took place, I think there were certain changes, in terms of personnel, but I don't recall any specific names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked about the presence of members of Dusko Malovic's unit at Vrace on -- on the front line when you were there in Vrace. My question is: Do you know how many members of the unit were engaged in that activity at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they were in Vrace, the whole unit was engaged in combat. I told you already that some individuals from that list, as far as I know, were never officially ... specifically, I have Bartola in mind, and I don't know whether there was anyone else. Officially, they were on the list. I know Bartola from Sarajevo. I think he used to box. But I never saw him in that unit. That is why it's difficult to mention any figures, but it's probably around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You saw 20 different members of that unit present in Vrace at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But not Bartola?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the man, but I never saw him up there. However, he seemed to be on the list of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned -- oh, you were -- I'll go back now to questions from yesterday, and this is at page 16 from yesterday's transcript. Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the meeting with representatives of my office, the OTP, in May of this year, with an investigator named Paul Grady, with Belinda Pidwell and an investigator, and how you had been given your transcript only at 8.00 the night before. It's my understanding, though, that the next morning you did report that you had read your transcript and made some corrections. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I said to them that I was able to read it through very fast, and I made notes of some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked, then, at page 18, about whether somebody had sent you a message concerning that meeting, somebody had sent you a message to the effect that you had to be cooperative or else you would be fired. Do you remember Mr. Zecevic asking about that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's not connected to that. That has to do with the interview in 2004, as far as I remember. But nobody sent me any messages then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're correct. It was concerning the interview in 2004 when you were going to be interviewed as a suspect. And you told him it wasn't anybody from the OTP who gave you that message, but it was -- at page 19, line 4, your answer was: "This was given to me indirectly, and it could have been conveyed by the lawyer Trivun." Is that Trivun Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought he was lawyer, an attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Trivun Jovicic is a lawyer. He's a Liaison Officer for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. Is that the person you're talking about who gave you that message?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I received it indirectly; that is, the document went from the Government Secretariat for Cooperation with the ICTY, through the chiefs of services, and they forwarded it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But where does Mr. Jovicic come in? You mentioned him specifically. Did he speak to you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovicic only briefly spoke to me earlier, before the interview I gave the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and did he indicate to you that you might be fired if you didn't cooperate with The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I thought that maybe he had spoken to people from the government. But I don't know where that message originated from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as I understood your answer yesterday, you had that impression; that's part of the reason you were worried, because you had the impression that you might be fired if you were seen to be non-cooperative. And my question now is: From whom did you get that impression? And if you feel like this is something we should go into private session for, we can.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have very bad experience from the previous period, maybe from 2001, because of "non-cooperation" with the international factor, and that referred directly to me when I was appointed director of the service. Then there were interventions to nullify the appointment. The prime minister could do so. And I got the message perfectly then. And then I resigned after 45 days in office. That's -- that -- that suffices, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to -- I have to press on this. You still haven't answered my question. When you were talking about this with Mr. Zecevic yesterday, he asked you: "So this warning, if I may call it that, was conveyed to you by another person" - other than someone from the OTP - "right?" And your answer was: "Yes." My question is: Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A man from the service. But I'll keep the name to myself. From my own service, the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked at page 21 and 22 about what happened to you in 1991 when you were removed from your position and -- and put in the position as commander in Marin Dvor, and Mr. Zecevic asked you if you were -- if it was true that you weren't the only professional police officer who had that kind of experience after the national parties came to power. And you said there were many like you that had that happen to them. My question is: Isn't it true that happened to professional policemen of -- of all three ethnicities, Serb, Croats, and Muslims? Professional policemen lost their jobs because political appointees were put in their place.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then Mr. Zecevic discussed with you the problems that you saw in your area in 1991 with distribution of weapons to these additional reserve police of Muslim ethnicity and the related problem of non-qualified persons being put in jobs like chief of the SJB, et cetera. And he, at page 28, said: "And this was particularly widespread among the Muslim community ..." And my question is: Are you saying it was a bigger problem in the Muslim community than the other two communities? Didn't they all have the same problems?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say may be right, but this concerned me personally, and what I was able to observed -- observe - and I not only observed it, but I only -- also made notes and documented it - I took lists from drawers and had a look at the names on those lists. And that's why I stand by my statement as correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you don't disagree that in other parts of Bosnia and some places, Croatians had the problem that Muslims and/or Serbs were getting weapons and higher number of reserve police and having appointees placed in jobs that had previously been held by people of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably right. But the individual peoples were in different positions. It was said that the military was Serb, although it wasn't, so that there was no need for additional ... if the army had remained Yugoslav, there would have been no need for any changes. But you know what happened to the army at a certain point in time; it started breaking up along ethnic lines. And then we know what followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. The situation I'm talking about now, though, was widespread and well-known, and that was part of the reason the federal inspectors, Mico Davidovic and I can't remember the name of the other man, came to Bosnia to investigate the situation; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand that their arrival -- or I didn't understand that the reason for their arrival was to conduct an investigation. As far as I know, there was agreement between Minister Delimustafic and the federal minister to have them come and act as a calming factor. They weren't all Serbs. There were also Bosniaks among them, such as Sead Rekic; the man had come from the federal SUP. Because the federal SUP was manned from all republics, and they had their term in office for a while. So they were supposed to -- to assess the situation and come up with solutions to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. But I understood that to address the situation they had to first find out what it was and that involved doing some investigation about the situation where a local politically-appointed SJB chief in many places was expanding the reserve police force by adding on dozens or hundreds of people of his own ethnicity, whether they were qualified or not, whether they were criminals or not, and giving them weapons. And that was part of what this federal inspection team was trying to find out about; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
