utterances.text: Thank you. At page 41, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about your -- your whereabouts in 1992 from the time that you joined the RS MUP. And could you clarify for me again when you first joined the RS MUP. I think you went to Pale on the 13th or 14th of April and met with Cedo Kljajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was certainly like that. I explained. I had some private business of my own at Pionirska Dolina, and I did some things on the way and returned from Pionirska. But I came to Vrace in my capacity of assistant on the 20th. I was corrected yesterday by Mr. Zecevic. And it was basically then that I assumed my post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then from the 20th of April until early June you were in Vrace, and then you went to Pale and Kalovita Brda?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were you that week between the 13th and 20th of April, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to my family, my parents, because my wife and our child had returned. They were staying at a village some 60 kilometres from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the witness 1D46.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Coming up on your screen in a minute is a document you were shown yesterday by Mr. Zecevic. It's the 15 May 1992 order regarding forming war units in the MUP. And I wanted to confirm that you did not see or receive a copy of this in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I think I didn't read it, and I think that Cedo Kljajic informed me of it. I may have read it subsequently, but I don't remember. I know, however, that Cedo told me that I was on some sort of war staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we have seen in document P160 that the record of the 11 July meeting in Belgrade, that the minister made a specific reference to this order by date and number. Do you remember him talking about it at the 11 July meeting in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. It was long ago. I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just for reference, that's at page 15 of the English and the B/C/S of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Zecevic at page 47, line 20 -- he said: "Tell me, Mr. Planojevic, the role of the ministry and the ministry administrations is first and foremost of instructive nature; right?" And your answer was: "Yes. They instruct and coordinate. That is their role." I'd like to have you take a look at something in Exhibit P530. We'll put that up on the screen. I'll tell you this is the Law on Internal Affairs for -- for the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 6 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look at Article 33. And my English translation reads: "The seat of the ministry shall" -- the first item is: "Directly execute activities pertaining to national security." And the second one says: "Monitor, direct, and coordinate the work of the centre of public security services and public security services." So, in addition to instructing and coordinating, the ministry is to monitor and direct the work of the CSBs and the SJBs; correct? It's not just instruct.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well ... you expect an answer from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like one, if I could, please.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says. I don't think that's in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll ask a kind of question that Judge Harhoff often asks. I know that's what it says, and we take that to mean that's the way it was supposed to work. Is that how it actually worked in real life?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we go back to the explanations of the conditions or circumstances - I don't think I need to repeat them - and what the conditions dictated, I think that what was done was the utmost possible, in terms of coordination and monitoring. But it -- please do not forget how we lived at those times and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. While I have the Law on Internal Affairs up, I'll ask you this question. At page 50, line 14, you were asked about the incident when you and Cedo Kljajic asked the minister to have Deputy Minister Momcilo Mandic removed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you agreed with Mr. Zecevic's proposal that there was a procedure for appointing the minister and deputy minister, and that was something that was a decision at higher level. I've looked at this Law on Internal Affairs. I see no reference to the position of a deputy minister or the appointment or removal of such a person. Can you tell me where in the law that is, or was, in 1992? Is it in some other law; or do you know?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the selection procedure for any minister, not only the minister of the interior, is the same, as well as that for selecting the deputy. There was something about that in the law, and I was also in a municipal administration body, which is basically a municipal level government, so I knew the provisions of the Law on Public Administration. I believe that you can find the relevant provisions in that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So can --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, at the time, I think the Law on Associated Labour was still in force. I'm not sure what exactly the law was called. But there was a law that regulated the relations and public administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So at the time that you made this suggestion, what was your personal understanding about who had the authority to remove the deputy minister, Mr. Mandic? Who did you think could do that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in every country, the prime minister is appointed by the -- did parliament, and parliament later on also confirms the cabinet. Here, I believe that it was upon the proposal of the prime minister. It was possible to remove him, given the wartime conditions. But I think that it must have been the prime minister to do that. Because if the -- if parliament cannot meet, cannot convene, then until the first session of parliament, the prime minister has the relevant powers. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking if you could please repeat the last sentence. The last thing we have is that "until the first session of parliament the prime minister has the relevant powers." And then you started another sentence, and they didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The state president has the powers of parliament, if parliament cannot convene, cannot meet. And I said that Momo Mandic couldn't be removed without the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understood your testimony, you knew and were friendly with the prime minister, Mr. Djeric. Did you ask him if he could do something about Momo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I took the opportunity when the minister was present at Vrace, and I considered it logical, because this was about his deputy, to request him to do that. At the time, I couldn't take forest-paths in my car -- with my car. There was an opportunity, I took it, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it -- you say you spoke to Minister Stanisic because he was there at Vrace, but you didn't speak to Mr. Djeric because you weren't able to drive to Pale and talk to him about Mr. Mandic; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no point in my going to see the prime minister because the minister had promised that he would tackle the issue with the most responsible people of the country. And then I don't even know if Momcilo Mandic had a decision appointing him to his position. Or if he only functioned by inertia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One thing I was confused about yesterday, your -- your accidental meeting of Mr. Stanisic when he was walking with the German Shepherd dog. Can you tell me where that took place and when that took place? Because I'm not clear if it -- that happened in June near Bistrica, or if it happened in October, or when you were in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is this relevant and important?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. It relates to who he saw when, in terms of security personnel. That's the only reason I'm asking. And I had understood him to say one thing before, and I just want to be sure I have my dates and meetings correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The encounter most probably took place in June, in front of the Bistrica hotel in October, in the forest close to the village where Mr. Stanisic's parents lived ... that's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in October, did you see any security personnel with Mr. Stanisic? In the forest.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Jasarevic was there as a driver, and Abazovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you saw those two with him in front of the Bistrica hotel in June as well?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came out of the hotel alone then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At page 63 from yesterday's transcript, you were talking about sending Mr. Borovcanin and Mr. Orasanin to Vogosca and Ilijas. And at line 12, you said: Yes, they'd gone there -- you had a correction - you said: "They were sent by Cedo." And then you went on to say: "Mico phoned [sic] me on the phone the following day. He asked me about some instruction, what he should do." Who is the Mico you're referring to there? I assume that's not Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Milomir Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were -- yesterday at page 67, you were shown the document of the two inspectors about their attempts to investigate the situation at Vogosca in connection with the stolen cars. And Mr. Zecevic asked you about the opinion expressed at the meeting by the SJB chief, Mr. Maksimovic. And you said there were many such examples of this kind of behaviour at the local levels. Can you give us a couple of other examples besides this one with Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We touched upon Teslic a minute ago. Then we also discussed Bijeljina and how many centre chiefs and station chiefs were removed in a short period of time. There was something in Foca, I believe, as well, because a commission was sent there. Members of the police station had been beaten up and kicked out of the premises. They forbade them to come back. It took a long time to set up the police station, to have it functioning properly. And the centre, too. I could go on. In any case, the entire police station personnel was beaten up and kicked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some so-called intervention unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I was looking for examples of where the SJB chiefs exercised that kind of attitude toward the higher levels of the MUP. Do you have any other examples of that, other than Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just enumerated the stations at which the removals occurred for that very reason, I believe. Of course, I'm no Einstein, to be able to cram it all into such a small head of mine. I'm not trying to be cynical. But even when I discuss things of yesterday, I start mixing them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That happens to me too. You -- were you aware of a police chief in Bosanski Samac named Stevo Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed that topic. I told you that I met the man during a session of the RS Assembly, which I think took place in Jahorina in 1993. I was able to link the events and developments with that man later on, whom I had met.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have about 20 more minutes, so perhaps this is a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the record, we reconvene for this final session today under Rule 15 bis, Judge Delvoie being absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to begin by showing you an exhibit in evidence, P406. And we've been talking about Stevo Todorovic. What you'll see on the screen in a moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is a confidential document, I'm reminded, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Then, Your Honour, can we not broadcast it but make it available for the witness. And thanks for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see this is a report by a couple of inspectors. You'll see their names in a minute on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is report based on their work done in connection with the Bosanski Samac Police Station. And I think you can see above their names and signatures the recommendations or proposed measures. And the first one is: "We recommend the removal of the chief of the Samac SJB because the Samac SJB has not functioned properly in any aspect of its work." And I'll inform you that the chief they're talking about was Stevo Todorovic. Were you aware of this recommendation from these inspectors? Did you ever hear about it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of this. I think I said yesterday, since I see the first name here in the signature block, I don't think that person was in service when I was in the administration at all; therefore, I presume that this was drafted later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I think this document is from -- from November of 1992, after you were no longer in the administration. How about the second inspector; did you know him? The second one named there.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you know him to be a professional and good at his job?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as far as you know, Stevo Todorovic was never removed from his position; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I only said that I saw him, I believe, in January of 1993. There was snow on the ground; that's why I say January. It was when the assembly met, and that's when I saw him at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've looked at this one before. It's a list of various MUP personnel and units that were nominated for various awards. And you remember we saw your name on this list as someone who was nominated for an award for the medal for service to the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could now look at page 12 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see number 91 on the list is Stevo Todorovic, chief of the Samac SJB. So not only was he not removed, he was given an award; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned earlier in your testimony that you had spoken to Mico Stanisic about being able to request assistance from the special unit if you needed it. And as I understood it, he -- he had approved that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you became aware of some of the circumstances in the Vogosca SJB, as we saw mentioned in that report from the two inspectors in mid-July, did you -- did you consider the possibility of asking the special unit to arrest anyone in connection with that? For example, Boro Radic. Was that something you considered?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not. And I need to explain why. I said that as of the 11th of July I no longer had my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about something that Mr. Zecevic raised at page 73, line 15. Yesterday he was asking you if there was any kind of attitude within the RS MUP, any attitude of discrimination versus non-Serbs in the RS MUP while you were there. And you said: "Absolutely not." Can you tell me, do you know or do you remember how many non-Serbs were employed by the RS in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the area in question. Perhaps you'd like me to be more specific? As far as I recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do you have a total number?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Very few. But I wanted to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anything about the area of Sarajevo, but I arrived in Banja Luka in 1993, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall what the name was, but there was a Bosniak who was in the class junior to mine and I came across him in the centre there. I didn't have access there, but I did run into him in down-town Banja Luka. I think it's Nijaz Selimovic; I think he's the chief of the police administration now. Where there was no serious combat, people stayed, throughout the war. And it is a small number of people though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only enumerated those I saw personally, and I cannot go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of transcript, I believe the witness gave the name of this Bosniak that he met is in the centre of -- security centre, CSB Banja Luka. And it said down-town Banja Luka. And this other, Nijaz Selimovic is from Gradiska. That's what the witness said. So, can this be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Planojevic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the highest position held by any non-Serb in the RS MUP in 1992, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of a single one in a senior position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Lastly, at page 75 yesterday, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the fact that there were numerous repeated instructions issued from the ministry to the field, stressing the need to obey the law for -- and for police to act in accordance with the laws and regulations. And his question was: "Isn't it true that due to the objective situation and the war, the Ministry of Interior, to make sure that it's get through to the lowest level - the SJBs - repeatedly sent out orders with basically the same contents?" Your answer was: "Yes, that's -- that's true. But you had to be flexible. And when I say 'flexible,' I mean that you had to balance things. Whether it was justified to, say, sacrifice a village, or not insist on things, and I've also explained the conditions which we worked." My question, my first question, is: Is one of the ones that these instructions were repeated frequently over time is because the minister and the ministry had information that they weren't being followed by some members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For objective reasons, which I won't repeat now, but as you could see, yourself, if an entire police station personnel is kicked out of -- off the premises, what possibility do have you left? Would you engage the whole special unit, which did happen in the case of Zvornik; would you take the whole unit to deal with such a problem? And I told you what the numerical strength and ratio was, especially in the area of Sarajevo. Or would you rather choose to try to keep the strategic positions. If you abandon a single position, you lose an entire area. It was, among others, for that reason why it was repeated. When we discussed things, then things come to mind. But I can't recall everything, and I can't now recall off the cuff all sorts of situations taking place. But it was mostly for those reasons that it was observed that the situation was not improving, and then it was insisted again. In Bijeljina, after I don't know how many removals of chiefs, in late 1992, finally there was some sort of situation in which Bosniaks could normally live in the town. But there were areas that were not close to areas of combat. Another problem was mass casualties. When I say "mass casualties," if you lost, say, a dozen men from the unit, you simply could not reign in all those relatives. They would not do it in full sight… retaliate. Or whether they would kick somebody from the apartment or not. I heard people speaking about Smoluca, a few thousand people being surrounded. Who could prevent people in Bijeljina from kicking some Bosniaks out? The only thing these people could do was fight each other. Say, a column of 5 or 6,000 people comes to Bijeljina, and there were such cases. I do not deny that that is a war crime, when a person who is a member of… However, try and put yourself in our shoes to try and tackle such a problem. I cannot recall everything, as I said, and it very much depends on what decision you will make at that moment, whether you shoot because there were armed people. There was convoy leaving Gorazde and 50 people are killed in ambush. You simply couldn't stop the hoards spraying bullets over all buildings because they believed they were left to their own devices, that they were betrayed. The opposite side, the enemy, no longer matters. They simply turned their rage against anyone. Then I tried to think what to say and then I might not say it. Maybe I'm not saying everything I wanted to say even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to what you're just saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, it's previous page, it's line 14: "... 5- or 6.000 people moved somewhere in Bijeljina. And it is a sort of war crime." It is not what witness said with that regard, so could you clarify that with witness. Because otherwise it's really unclear, this sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, you heard what Mr. Pantelic just said. Do you want to help us with that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that it too was a war crime. But those, the new arrivals, were kicking out Bosniaks. There were such instances. So I place both sides in that context which was not viable. If someone asked me, Go ahead and deal with the situation, I'd run because I wouldn't be able to deal with it. There were many killed. There were hundreds of people who came into new areas with their children. We can, of course, view things from our perspective here today. But at the time, it was incomprehensible. I have to go on. I'm sorry. There was a clash between Bosniaks and Croats in Vares, and there was 6- or 7.000 people leaving the area who came at the plateau at Nisici. And then you find yourself in a position where your work-mate comes to, say, Visegrad, but you advise him to go because I don't know whether I can guarantee his safety overnight. Whether I decided correctly ... then he came to Visegrad from Vares, someone gives me a call asking me to guarantee their safety, then the police call him, he says, As far as we are concerned, we'll do everything to protect you, but we advise you to move on to Belgrade, and he did. I'd lie if I were to say that we could -- that Croat. But we -- I believe that it was wiser to tell him to move on. You can judge me, but I'm simply -- sometimes you deal with the situation because you believe it to be the more favourable, and then we can discuss why this Croat had no freedom in Vares, or in Visegrad. I'm going back to some things that may be unrelated, but I'm trying to picture the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. I want to try and ask you two very specific questions here, and then I'll be finished. As part of the objective situation at the time - and I think that includes everything you've just been telling us about the war, about the combat, about the shortage of manpower on the Serb side - was part of the objective situation that there was a more lenient attitude towards some of these paramilitary groups because, to the extent that they were willing and able to engage in combat, they were needed, and, therefore, they might have been treated more leniently than they would have been in non-wartime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, if I might interpose that question. A more lenient attitude on whose part?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the part of the authorities in terms of overlooking any crimes they might have committed.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I've been explaining all the time, when I said flexible. I'll give you another example. What Grbavica meant, or Vrace, in my statement that I gave in 2004, I said, roughly, that there was a situation where I was assistant minister at headquarters, and a hundred metre across the road that passes along the school compound there were the lines of the enemy. But no -- not one man was wounded or killed in our compound. And that's why people were weighing or were -- were trying to make up their mind. Was it actually war or wasn't it? It was May and there wasn't really any heavy fighting, only occasional shots. People didn't want to leave their apartments. Few people in Sarajevo wanted to leave everything they had acquired in their lives behind, including the Serbs, until they went -- until they had gone through their ordeal. And when you get hold of someone who can carry a rifle, then you keep them. People are brought in from the surrounding areas. And, I repeat, I was only a hundred metres away from the rifles of the enemy. And in such a situation, who would dare go about and arrest people? And you know what kind of people you get. Some are more than ready to -- to kill you, to kill their commanders. I gave you an example. So who would dare stand up to them? So I -- I hope that this was at least an attempt to explain how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you have explained it, and that leads to my last question. And I think you've answered it, in part. Did this situation in this circumstance where it sounds like you're saying you needed all the able-bodied, armed men you had to fight, did that lead, in part, to an attitude by many Serbs, including Serbs in the police, of: Serbs shouldn't arrest Serbs, especially Serbs who committed crimes against non-Serbs, because you needed Serbs to fight? Would you agree that that was the attitude of many at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you go back to my dispatch - and I explained what it means to -- to secure evidence - I was very much aware that much time would elapse until we can -- although things have been documented, although you have proved something, much time will elapse until we could start prosecuting. And that's why, to come back to your question, were there such individuals? Yes, of course, there were. And we know that any way. What can I add to that? But the majority, especially talking about professional police officers, acted responsibly and did much more than is obvious. And when you meet a Croat or Bosniak in Sarajevo nowadays, they are likely to remember things. So that's why I'm saying that much more was done than is obvious at first glance. Because even today I walk the streets of that town without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Planojevic. I don't have any more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. Your testimony is now at an end, and you're released as a witness. We wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I believe, according to the schedule I've seen, we're all mornings next week in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I was going to indicate I have no more witnesses to call today, so I'd ask that we stop for the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So we adjourn to Monday morning. I wish everyone a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of November, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.58 p.m.,
